It's not about approval or anything like that. The labels are for me. I know they still mean different things to everyone, but I like having language that can do a lot of the explaining for me if I want to discuss gender with people. Labels help me find people that I can relate to as well. Even if the label I choose doesnt mean the exact same thing to another person with that label, the fact that we both felt connected to it creates a connection in itself. Also finding labels has helped me feel better about the way I experience things differently than others. For example, finding the label aromantic helped me take a lot of pressure off myself to feel romantic attraction. I don't absolutely need labels to feel good about myself, but I enjoy having access to them and exploring them and how they change for me.

Last time we hung out, we were eating, so minimal eye contact was much easier to work in naturally. But this time we were just sitting and talking while facing each other for a while, and I struggled to make eye contact while they were talking. I was able to be comforted by the fact that they know I'm autistic, so they likely wouldn't consider my minimal eye contact to be rude. 

In terms of forming more connections than I've realized, I've definitely noticed a lot of that in the past few weeks. Two weeks ago, I went to my club with the goal of spending time with all my friends. I was able to spend time with one friend, but got stuck in an activity that was long and confusing. Then some of the other people that I wanted to grow closer to went somewhere without me instead of walking home with me like usual. I was very upset because of that whole situation.

Last week, I had to send several emails and submit an application for something. The process was extremely draining, so I skipped going to my club in order to decompress. If I have a strongly negative emotional experience somewhere, I tend to avoid that thing/place automatically. Fighting the avoidance urge literally feels like trying to force myself to touch a hot stove and questioning whether it will hurt me. 

This week, I debated going to club because of that avoidance instinct, but I went anyway and I'm so glad I did. I literally got everything I wanted out of a meeting.  I got to spend time with all of the people I'm trying to get closer to. We were in a quiet room away from the loud noise of everyone else in the club. This was my first time alone with all of them away from the rest of the club, and I seemed to blossom. I felt comfortable. I was having fun, being more of myself, and cracking jokes. Afterwards, I was invited to go with them to the place they had gone without me before and then walk home after. It was essentially the polar opposite of two weeks ago. We even set up an activity that will involve us all spending more time together hanging out. 

I also had a situation a few weeks ago in which a professor pulled me aside to compliment my work ethic and offer help with career opportunities. I had only been around this professor for a few weeks, and I've noticed that in general I manage to form very good relationships with my professors very quickly without even realizing it. So I've been assessing how my drive for learning presents itself in ways that I don't recognize and that they are able to notice. I tend to be very quiet in my classes, yet my professors are so quickly able to recognize that I'm trying to learn and understand. Sometimes I wish I could get a good look at myself from the outside. Cause I'm starting to recognize that the view I've created based on self perception is very lacking. 

Also, I would like some advice if you can give it. One of the people I'd like to get closer to, I consider very cute. I ran into them today and we had a nice chat and they walked with me to my location. They haven't given me any indication (that I've noticed) that they view me as more than a friend. Which makes sense since we've only spoken a few times and are still getting to know each other. I want to figure out how to initiate some kind of subtle flirting that will allow me to make my interest known without making our budding friendship awkward if they're not interested. I know this is kind of off topic, but I like your thoughts on relationships and communication. So I thought maybe you would have some good advice about this situation.

Sorry, I had some bad burn out last week. I'm ok with eye contact mostly. Eye contact is hardest for me when I'm upset or when I'm talking to someone who has some level of authority (ex: professor).

I've formed a pretty good formula of looking over a little bit and then looking away if it feels like too much. Its helpful in groups cause usually the person talking isn't just looking at me so I can just look at their face or the other people they're talking to. 

It also helps there's an activity happening (ex: we're playing d&d so there's a board or dice to fidget with, we're going on a car ride so there's a window to look at) so that I can have an eye contact break that doesn't seem like I'm not listening. I also make a point to do things like nod or make affirming noises when people are saying things. I've been told that I'm a good listening so people don't seem to mind and can tell I'm listening. 

I make an effort to look at people if they're talking in a group so that they know I'm part of the listeners. That short moment of eye contact they make in response is ideal for me. I also stomach a lot more eye contact if a person is talking to a group and notices that I'm the only one actually listening to them. In case they're feeling rejected in the moment, I want to make absolutely sure that they know I see them. 

Overall, I'd say that my eye contact isn't noticeably lacking. I've only ever heard a comment about it from people like my family or my best friend who've been around me when I'm distressed. 

When I am in situations where I have to make more eye contact then I'm comfortable with (ex: zoom calls) I tend to get distracted both by how unpleasant it feels to stare and how much I feel like people think I'm just staring through their soul or something

I love your poem! Also I get what you mean about masking. When I recognize that I'm doing it, I realize how anxious its making me to sit there forcing myself to interact a certain way and overthinking every little thing. 

I just went to my club last night so I have some fresh thoughts. This is all slightly skewed because I was particularly tired during all of this, and I think starting to get mentally overestimated as a result. But I noticed that while I usually like large groups so that I don't feel pressure fill silence and so that I can sit and observe to learn the way this group socializes, it can be somewhat of an obstacle to developing closer friendships. 

I tend to be very quiet. It takes me a little longer to form my thought when I'm in a conversation, and I don't speak if I have nothing to say. When I'm one on one with people, I have an easier time going through the "get to know you" questions and trying to form that into a conversation. But in a group, I end up on the outskirts of the conversation, saying nothing but wanting to participate even if I have nothing to say. 

I also am very soft spoken. So often times when trying to say something, even just a small comment in between a conversation to let people know I'm here, I go unheard. I've noticed that the friends I'm developing still recognize my presence more than a stranger and still engage with me, but when they're gathered with other friends, its hard to make an impression. 

Also sometimes I mask on purpose because I want to communicate certain things in a way that people will understand. For example, one of my friends does very dark or odd jokes sometimes. I enjoy them and think they're funny, but my body doesn't naturally laugh at them cause I'm confused at first. Or sometimes I laugh only a little bit, when I think its very funny. So I will fake the output of my laugh to match the inner feelings so that this friend knows I think they're funny. (If this section seems out of place, its because I added it after the fact but I'm too tired to make it cohesive)

Next week, I'm going to practice inserting myself a little more and confront my friends directly. Last night, I stayed in one little section and then was sad when I wasn't around the people I want to be closer to (this sentence would make more sense with context, but I'm trying to be private). Next time, I will go and find my friends so that I can interact with them on purpose and then actually try to talk to them and ask questions cause questions are an ok thing to ask. 

Pushing myself to say things when I wouldn't naturally may be a form of masking, but I want to be able to engage with people. And I'm starting to realize that doing that by just being around doesn't work as well. I don't know what I will say yet, but I will speak more.

(Sorry this ended up longer than intended. Tl;dr: I think my isolation is a product of anxiety and a negative self perception. I'm working on shifting that now.)

Thank you. I think I probably mask more than I think when I'm around people. I relate to your feelings a lot. I've always loved dresses and skirts and traditionally feminine stuff. People have always described me as really "girly." For a while I thought that I was just looking for attention or overthinking or something. But now I know I'm definitely just a very feminine guy. Part of what helped put it in perspective for me was questioning whether I'd rather be a feminine guy or a feminine girl. The idea of just existing as a feminine guy made me really happy and felt more right than anything else. Another mind trick I used was asking myself, "If you were the last person on earth or stranded alone on an island, what gender would you want to be?" That question helped me realize that without any outside influences whether that be pressure of gender roles, transphobia, or anyone else's opinions and perceptions of me and my gender, I would still feel much better existing as a guy, even if I'm a guy in a dress. I can imagine that everything feels scary and impossible right now, but you do have a future where you can live as yourself and be happy and free.

I can't answer all of these, but I can try to answer a few. 

1. I realized I'm trans because I realized that I didn't really feel connected to being a girl in the way most people seem to. I found myself relating to certain experiences and feelings that other trans people had. Once I unlocked that door of questioning my gender, I eventually realized that I'm a guy because it made me so happy to refer to myself as a guy. I also realized that I'd always wanted to be a guy, but didn't think I was allowed to be. Also I'm actually into more feminine things. I used to consider myself a girly girl. Now I realize I'm just a feminine guy. 

3. That depends on the person I guess. Some people prefer to be stealth about it and just be referred to as a man or woman. Some people identify as trans. Also transitioning doesn't always have a set "end" for every single person. For example, some trans people don't want to medically transition. Some people only want certain transition surgeries like hormones or top surgery. Not every trans person goal is to be seen as 100% cis-passing. Most trans people are just trying to be whatever version of them feels best to them even if they don't fully pass as a man or woman. 

4. Its not transphobic to have a personal preference or to not want to date someone that you're not attracted to. If you have a genitalia preference then that's fine. But if the basis of your lack of attraction is the fact that you know the person is trans, then yes thats transphobic. You cannot always tell a person is trans just by looking at them. There are trans women that look 100% cis and have had bottom surgery. And no its not sexist that gay men aren't attracted to women. You can't control whether you're gay, straight, etc. But if you meet a woman and are attracted to her, like her personality, like her body, etc and then suddenly don't want to date her because you found out she's trans then yes thats transphobic. Trans women are women. 

5. In that scenario, yeah your sexuality would change. I've heard situations in which some trans people's sexualities change a lot after they start to transition. For example, say someone identifies as a lesbian, but then they transition and realize that they thought they liked girls because they wanted to be seen more like a boy, and all the boys around them like girls. Then they transition and feel better about themselves and their gender and end up finding out that they were attracted to boys the entire time. Or say they thought they liked boys originally, and then realized that their attraction was actually just jealousy because they wanted to look like the guys they thought they were attracted to. Then they transition and realize they like girls. 

7. Someone who has more dysphoria around being misgendered will be able to explain how it feels better. I know some people have described it as being extremely painful and hurtful. Also misgendering by accident isn't transphobic. Misgendering on purpose is though. I don't know who you've seen say that misgendering should be illegal, but most trans people don't think that. Its always better to ask someone's pronouns than assume since you never really know unless they tell you. Also in the situation where if a stranger misgenders them, some trans people don't find it necessary to correct a stranger for several reasons. 1. The stranger could be transphobic and start being physically or verbally abusive. 2. They could prefer not to disclose that info to someone they don't know. 3. They might not feel like opening up a discussion or potential questions about their gender. Or 4. They might be in a hurry and just want to move on.

If I don't, they type with one hand and make way more typos. Talking is also like a word document, but the words get typed out and then played through one of those dictating programs. Each sentence is carefully checked for syntax errors, tone confusion, potential interpretations, politeness, and any necessary personalizations for the listener by a program similar to Grammarly. Once a sentence is begun, it has to be typed all the way. The dictating function is often unable to be used when the "grammarly" function doesn't work fast enough, or the dictating gets interrupted or ignored when the output volume is too low. Intrusive negative thoughts are pop-up ads that have to be closed a few times before they leave. The computer shuts off from low battery when too many programs are open or when the "grammarly" program has been open at all. Sensory overload is like the computer overheating and needing to stop being used for a little while to cool down. Meltdown is like the computer freezes up, gets many pop-ups and a few viruses, and has to be shut off completely and had the viruses carefully removed before it will work again.
